threads.thread_goal: Align on current sorting workflow, main bottlenecks and safety pain points.

messages.text: Kicking off for Mixed-Waste Sorting Line Safety and Efficiency Upgrade. For this thread, can everyone walk through how the mixed-waste line actually runs today and where it hurts most? I will use this to move T1 forward and feed into the layout sketch in A6 later. Please call out: 1) where material backs up, 2) where you see most contamination, 3) any spots that feel risky for slips, cuts, or forklift conflicts.

From my shift: 1) Biggest backup is just before the manual picking station when the infeed belt runs faster than we can pull cardboard and plastics. 2) Contamination is worst in the mixed bulky section, lots of bags with hidden liquids and small electronics. 3) Risky spots: wet floor around the drain near the compactor and tight turn where the forklift comes in to swap full cages. I can help map this for T1 if you want.

On nights we get a lot of bags piling up right at the hopper because no one is at the pre-sort for the first half hour. I also see people tossing whole bags with liquids straight on the belt, so we get splashes further down. Not sure if that is a bottleneck or just bad habit, but it slows us when we have to stop and clean.

Day shift view: 1) When the forklift is swapping out full metal cages near the end of the line, we have to pause picking because the aisle is blocked. That creates a wave of backlog. 2) Sharp metal pieces mixed with plastics at the picking station slow everyone down because we stop to find proper containers. 3) The step up to the picking platform is worn and easy to trip on when carrying heavy bags.

From the recycling side, contamination hotspots: 1) Black bags with mixed food and small WEEE, especially near the middle of the belt. 2) Liquids from paint cans and oil containers that were not drained. 3) Batteries and small electronics ending up in general waste tubs. These also link to hazardous handling later, but for now they are slowing us because we stop the belt to pull them out safely.

Adding to what others said: cleaning is hard to keep up with around the infeed and under the belt. When we do not sweep between loads, bits of glass and wet cardboard build up and people slip or twist ankles. It is not exactly a bottleneck, but when someone falls or we stop to clean, the line is down for a while.

Thanks all, this is helpful. For T1 I am sketching the current flow for each shift: infeed hopper -> pre-sort bags -> main belt picking -> metal cage area -> compactor. I will mark: 1) infeed to pre-sort speed mismatch, 2) manual picking overload, 3) forklift swap zone, 4) wet floor by compactor. I will drop a first version into A6 so we can all look at the same picture.

When you add to A6, can you separate day and night shifts on the map? On nights, we run with fewer people, so the pre-sort gap that 41356 mentioned is bigger. That might change which bottlenecks we tackle first.

Yes, nights are different. Also, the forklift driver sometimes parks the cage right in front of the emergency exit for a few minutes. It is not long, but it feels off. Maybe that is more for the layout discussion, but I wanted to flag it.

On the forklift side, the tight turn is because the containers are too close to the belt. If we shift the metal cages half a meter away in the new A6 layout, we could keep the aisle clear and still reach them. That would also reduce the time we block the pickers.

For the map in T1, can we mark where hazardous items usually show up on the belt? For example, batteries tend to be in the middle third, paint cans near the start. That will help later when we design the hazardous guide and also when we pick the pilot area.
Do we also want to note where we store cleaning tools on A6? Right now brooms and squeegees are scattered, so when there is a spill we waste time looking for them.

Good point. I will add typical spots for batteries, paint cans, and oil containers on the A6 map. That will also show where we slow down most to deal with them. Looking at what everyone shared, the main slowdowns seem to be: 1) infeed vs pre-sort staffing, 2) manual picking overload and contamination, 3) forklift cage swap zone. Are we missing any big one that affects most shifts?

From my side, those three cover most of the delays. The wet floor and cleaning gaps are serious but feel more like safety and housekeeping that we can handle with a better routine rather than a core flow bottleneck.
Agree. If we fix those three, contamination and rework should drop a lot. The hazardous items are part of the manual picking overload anyway, so they fit under that second point.
Works for me. Maybe we can treat the emergency exit blockage as part of the forklift cage swap issue so it is not forgotten.
Yes, those three are the main ones I see too.

Ok, summarising so we can move on: we will focus first on 1) infeed to pre-sort mismatch and early bag handling, 2) overload and contamination at the manual picking station, 3) forklift cage swap zone including emergency exit access. I will mark these as the top three bottlenecks on A6 and in the T1 notes. Next, we need to pick which section of the line we use as the pilot area for changes. My suggestion is the stretch from pre-sort through the first half of the picking station, since that is where most of these issues start. Any objections before we lock that in?
No objection. That area is easier to adjust without stopping the whole line, and we can still run the rest as usual.
Works for me too. That section also gives us a good view of contamination patterns for when we design the SOP and checklist later.
Fine by me. Just keep in mind nights have fewer people there, so any changes should still work with a smaller crew.
Great, then we will use the pre-sort plus first half of the picking station as the pilot area. I will highlight that zone clearly on A6 so everyone knows what we are adjusting first.

threads.thread_goal: Define and lock the standard sorting and contamination control procedure.

messages.text: I have put a first draft of the mixed-waste sorting SOP into A1, based on T2. It covers: pre-sort bag opening, pulling out recyclables, handling liquids and dangerous items, and when to stop the belt. Can you all read through and comment here on anything that does not match how we actually work, or steps that feel unclear or too long for a shift huddle?

I went through A1. Overall it matches the flow we mapped in A6. A few notes: 1) In pre-sort, can we be more explicit that all bags with liquids should be opened and drained into the right container before going on the belt? 2) For small electronics, maybe add a simple rule like: anything with a plug, cable, or battery goes into the WEEE tub. 3) The stop-the-belt section is good but might be long for posters; we can highlight the top triggers for A2 later.

From a shift view, the steps are clear, but the wording in the cleaning and contamination part might be heavy for some of the crew. Could we simplify phrases like 'segregate incompatible waste streams' to something like 'keep food, metals, and electronics in separate tubs'?

I got a bit lost in the section about liquids. It says to drain containers but I am not sure where exactly. Maybe add a line about which drain or tray to use so we do not pour near the compactor again.
Agree with the others. Also, could we add a short reminder about PPE in the SOP, like gloves and eye protection when opening bags with liquids? It links to T10 but a quick note here would help.

On the contamination side, I like the idea of a checklist in A2. For the SOP, maybe we can keep the main flow simple and push the detailed checks into that checklist so people can run through it each load.

Thanks for the feedback. I will update A1 to: 1) spell out that all liquid containers are opened and drained into the designated tray at pre-sort, not near the compactor, 2) add the simple rule for anything with plug, cable, or battery, 3) simplify the language in the contamination section as 204917 suggested. Then we can pull the key checks into A2 for T3.

For A2, I suggest we keep it to a short list that can be done in under a minute per load. My first pass for must-have items: 1) Bags opened and obvious liquids drained in tray, 2) Visible electronics and batteries pulled, 3) Sharp metals separated into metal cage, 4) Floor around infeed clear and dry, 5) PPE on before starting. We can test this in the pilot area for T3.
Those five look ok to me. Maybe add something about checking that the WEEE tub is not overflowing before starting a new load, otherwise we end up stacking stuff on the side.
I like the short list. Could we merge the floor check with a quick look at the emergency exit path in the pilot area? It is fast to glance and it avoids surprises.

Ok, so for A2 must-use items on every load we have: 1) Bags opened and liquids drained in tray, 2) Electronics and batteries pulled to WEEE tub, 3) Sharp metals to metal cage, 4) Floor and emergency exit path clear and dry, 5) PPE on, 6) WEEE tub not overflowing. Anything else that absolutely needs to be on every load, or can we keep the rest as optional checks?
Maybe one more: check that the right tubs and cages are in place and labelled before starting. When labels are missing, people guess and that adds contamination.
Agree with adding the tubs and labels check. Beyond that, I would keep it as is so it stays quick.
Sounds good. So we lock those seven as the must-use items on A2 for every load, and anything else can go into a weekly or shift-start check instead.

I have now updated A1 with the simpler wording, the liquid draining tray location, the plug/cable/battery rule, and a short PPE reminder. Unless anyone spots a major gap, I suggest we treat this as the version to roll out in the pilot area first, then tweak if needed after a week.
I re-read A1 after your edits. It is clear enough for toolbox talks and matches what we discussed. I am ok to use it in the pilot.
Looks fine to me too. The liquid part is much clearer now.

I am also good with the updated A1. It lines up with the bottlenecks we picked and should be easy to explain using the script later. Let us mark this version as approved for rollout in the pilot area, with the understanding we can still adjust after we see it in use.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on new layout, rotation plan and cleaning routine for the pilot area.

messages.text: I have added a proposed layout sketch for the pilot area into A6, covering pre-sort, first half of the picking station, and the forklift cage zone, as part of T4. I also drafted a simple rotation pattern and put it into A8 for T12, plus a first pass at a cleaning and inspection list in A4 for T6. Can you all review and comment on: 1) any unsafe forklift paths or blocked exits, 2) whether the rotation feels realistic, 3) if the cleaning list is doable within the shift without stopping the line for more than short windows?

On A6, moving the metal cages half a meter away from the belt and keeping a straight forklift path works well. It gives enough clearance and keeps the emergency exit open. Only tweak I would suggest is marking a no-park zone in front of the exit so drivers do not leave cages there even for a short time.

Looking at A8, the rotation pattern that swaps people between heavy bag opening and lighter picking every hour seems fair. We just need to make sure there is always someone experienced at pre-sort on nights. Maybe mark one position as 'must be experienced' so supervisors know who to assign.
For the rotation in A8, I worry that swapping every hour might be too often on nights when we are short. It takes us a bit to settle into a spot. Maybe 2-hour blocks would be easier to manage.
On A4, the cleaning list looks ok, but the mid-shift deep clean under the belt might be hard to do while running. Could we move that to shift change or a planned short stop so we do not rush it?
Agree with 489662. Also, for A4, we should tie some checks to contamination control, like wiping the liquid tray and checking that the WEEE tub area is clean, so it supports A2 and the SOP.
Good call on the no-park zone. I will add a marked area on A6 and note it in T4 that cages cannot be left in front of the exit, even briefly.

On A8, I can adjust the rotation so that one pre-sort position is tagged as 'experienced operator' and does not rotate as often. For nights, we can also switch to 2-hour blocks as 41356 suggested, while keeping 1-hour blocks on days where we have more people.
That works for me. As long as the heavy tasks still rotate across the shift, 2-hour blocks on nights are fine.
Yes, 2-hour blocks will be easier to manage. I am ok with that plan.

For A4, let us move the deep clean under the belt to shift change and a planned short stop, and keep mid-shift to quicker tasks: sweep around infeed, wipe liquid tray, check WEEE and metal areas, and confirm floor and exit path are clear. That should keep us within the 2-hour stop limit overall.
Yes, that list is realistic. We can fit those mid-shift checks between loads without much downtime.
Linking the liquid tray and WEEE area checks to A2 is a good idea. That way the checklist and cleaning routine reinforce each other.
One more layout detail on A6: can we add a small marked spot for cleaning tools near the infeed, so brooms and squeegees are always in the same place? That will speed up spill response.
Yes, I will add a cleaning tools station to A6 and include a quick check in A4 that tools are present and in good condition at shift start.
With these tweaks, the layout in A6 looks safe and practical to me, and the rotation in A8 covers all key positions without overloading anyone. I am ok to use this setup in the pilot area.
Same here. The forklift path is clear, exits are open, and the rotation should help with heavy tasks. No further comments from me.
Ok, then we will confirm the new workstation layout and forklift paths in A6 for the pilot section, including the no-park zone, cleaning tools station, and adjusted cage positions.

For the cleaning and inspection routine, we will go with the updated A4: shift-start checks including tools and exits, mid-shift quick clean around infeed, liquid tray, WEEE and metal areas, and shift-change deep clean under the belt during a short planned stop. I suggest the shift supervisor signs off the A4 checklist at the end of each shift, based on what the team has ticked off.
I agree with having the supervisor sign off A4. That keeps it consistent across shifts.
Works for me. We can fill in A4 during the shift and hand it over for sign-off at the end.
Great, then we will treat the updated A4 as the approved daily cleaning and inspection routine for the pilot area, with shift supervisors signing off each completed checklist.

threads.thread_goal: Lock hazardous waste handling rules and incident reporting process.

messages.text: I have drafted the hazardous waste handling and storage guide in A3 for T5, and a simple incident and near-miss quick reference in A5 for T7. The guide lists common hazardous items we see on the line and where to store them; the quick reference covers when and how to report spills, mis-sorted hazardous items, and injuries. Please review and comment on anything that does not match what you see on the line or feels hard to follow in the moment.

On A3, the list of hazardous items looks right: batteries, paint cans, oil containers, aerosols, small electronics. One suggestion: for draining oil and paint, can we be very clear about using the dedicated tray and not the floor drain near the compactor? Also, maybe add a simple picture or description of the storage zones so people can match them on the floor.

A3 looks good overall. For storage, can we add a note about keeping incompatible items apart, like not stacking batteries with liquids? Even a simple rule like 'batteries in their own box, liquids in drums' would help.
I am a bit unsure about the part in A3 that mentions labelling. It says to label containers, but I do not know what exactly to write. Maybe give an example label text so we do it the same way.

On A5, the steps are clear but maybe we can shorten them. For example, instead of a long paragraph, we could have: 1) make area safe, 2) tell supervisor, 3) fill quick card, 4) place card in box. That would be easier to remember during a busy shift.
For A5, can we add a specific example for a forklift-related near miss, like almost hitting a cage or person, so drivers know that also needs reporting?

Good points. I will update A3 to: 1) state clearly that all draining of oil and paint happens in the dedicated tray at pre-sort, never near the compactor, 2) add simple diagrams or descriptions of the battery box, liquid drum, and WEEE cage zones, 3) include a basic label example like 'Used batteries only' or 'Waste oil only'.

I will also add the simple separation rule you suggested: batteries in their own box, liquids in drums, aerosols in a separate crate, and small electronics in the WEEE cage. That should keep incompatible items apart without going into too much technical detail.

For A5, I like the four-step version. Maybe we can standardise it as: 1) make safe, 2) tell supervisor, 3) fill card, 4) drop card in box. Then add two or three examples: spill of oil, battery found in general waste, forklift near miss.
Yes, that four-step version is easy to remember. We can also mention in toolbox talks that near misses count, not just actual injuries or spills.
Thanks for adding the label examples. That will help a lot. With that, A3 makes sense to me.
I am happy with the four steps and the examples you listed. That is about the right amount of detail for a quick reference like A5.
The forklift near-miss example is important. Maybe phrase it as 'forklift or cage came closer than one arm length to a person or exit' so it is concrete.

I have now updated A5 with the four standard steps and added three examples: oil spill at pre-sort, battery found in general waste tub, and forklift passing too close to a person or exit. Unless anyone sees a gap, I suggest we use this as the standard incident and near-miss process for the pilot area.

I have re-read A3 and A5 after your edits. The hazardous guide now clearly lists items, draining steps, storage zones, and labels, and the incident quick reference has a simple four-step process with clear examples. From my side, these are ready to use in the pilot, and we can still ask the health and safety officer to review A3 for compliance.
Agreed. A3 and A5 are clear enough for the crew. Getting a quick check from health and safety on A3 is a good idea, but we can already start using the rules in the pilot.
I am ok with using these versions as our standard in the pilot area.

Then let us treat the current A3 as the agreed hazardous handling and storage guide for the sorting area, pending a quick compliance check by health and safety, and A5 as the agreed incident and near-miss process everyone follows.

threads.thread_goal: Plan training huddles, PPE needs and go-live date for new routines.

messages.text: I have drafted a toolbox talk script for the new sorting, cleaning, and reporting routines in A7 for T8. It covers the updated SOP in A1, the contamination checklist in A2, the cleaning list in A4, and the incident quick reference in A5. It is about 15 minutes. We also need to finalise PPE and signage needs from T10 and agree a go-live date for the pilot. Please review A7 and share: 1) anything that feels too long or unclear, 2) PPE or signs we are missing, 3) any constraints on timing for go-live.

A7 reads well. To keep it within 15 minutes, maybe we can focus on three key messages: 1) how to sort and handle liquids and electronics (A1), 2) the must-do checks on A2, 3) the four steps from A5. For cleaning, we can just point to A4 and explain when we do shift-start, mid-shift, and shift-change tasks.
I like that the script in A7 has questions to ask the crew. Maybe add one simple check question about where to drain liquids and where to put batteries, so we know people got those parts.

On PPE and signage for T10, we will need: gloves and eye protection for bag opening and liquid handling, safety shoes and hi-vis for everyone on the line, and maybe cut-resistant sleeves for those handling sharp metals. For signs, we should have clear labels for the hazardous storage zones from A3, the no-park zone near the exit, and a poster with the four incident steps from A5.

Agree with 489662. For forklift drivers, we should also make sure hi-vis is mandatory and add a sign reminding about the no-park zone and near-miss reporting. That can sit near the cage area shown in A6.

On timing, if we want to start the pilot next week, we should run the toolbox talk on each shift at least once before go-live. That means we need final A7 and the PPE and signs in place a couple of days before.

I will tighten A7 around those three key messages and add the two check questions 41356 suggested about liquids and batteries. That should keep us within 15 minutes while still covering the essentials.

For T10, I will compile a list of PPE by task: 1) bag opening and liquids: gloves, eye protection, cut sleeves, safety shoes, hi-vis, 2) picking: gloves, safety shoes, hi-vis, 3) forklift: safety shoes, hi-vis. For signage, we will list: hazardous zones from A3, no-park zone and forklift rules near the cages on A6, contamination checklist poster from A2, and incident steps from A5.

If we aim for go-live mid next week, we could run toolbox talks on days Monday and Tuesday, and on nights Tuesday and Wednesday. That gives us time to catch most people before we switch the pilot area over.
That schedule works for nights. We just need the posters and signs up before the first night talk so we can point at them.
The PPE list by task looks right to me. We should send it to the health and safety officer so they can confirm and arrange any missing items.
For signage, can we also add a simple map near the pilot area showing the hazardous storage zones and the no-park area, based on A6 and A3? That will help new staff.
On educating new staff, I can draft a short guideline for T11 that uses the same examples from A1, A2, and A3, so we are consistent between toolbox talks and on-the-job coaching.

Given the training schedule you suggested, how about we set the pilot go-live for next Thursday at the start of day shift? That gives us Monday to Wednesday for toolbox talks and for health and safety to confirm PPE and signage.
Next Thursday start of day shift works for me.
Fine by nights as well, as long as we get our talks done before then.
I am ok with next Thursday as go-live for the pilot.
Ok, then we will set next Thursday, start of day shift, as the go-live date for the new sorting, cleaning, and reporting routines in the pilot area.

On PPE and signage, we will go with the list we outlined: PPE by task as in T10, plus signs for hazardous zones, no-park area, contamination checklist, and incident steps. I will send this list to the health and safety officer today so they can confirm and arrange any missing items before go-live.
That covers what I had in mind for PPE and signs.
Same here. Once health and safety confirms, we can treat that as the final list.
Great, then we will treat the PPE and signage list from T10 as confirmed for go-live, subject to health and safety confirming any ordering details.
